result: Two gata3 transgenic lines, Tg(gata3:loxP-DsRed-loxP:GFP) and Tg(gata3:Gal4), were generated via BAC transgenesis and label V2b neurons throughout the larval zebrafish spinal cord, with additional expression in brain, hindbrain, and non-nervous tissues including the pronephric duct.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 describe the generation and expression pattern of the transgenic lines. The manuscript provides direct evidence through methods description, imaging (Figure 1A), and citation for pronephric duct expression. The transgenic line validation via in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1) further supports these claims.

result: V2b neurons exhibit stereotyped anatomical features: each hemisegment contains ~17 V2b somata, all traced neurons (n=59) project ipsilateral, caudal axons (2-15 segments long) with no rostral projections beyond the segment of origin, and midbody neurons have the longest axons. Axons originate ventrally, project laterally into white matter, display en passant boutons, and extend collaterals medially.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 and C95-C99, C119-C120 collectively describe V2b anatomy with quantitative data (mean ± SD, n=59 neurons, statistical tests with p-values). The manuscript provides direct anatomical observations via single-cell labeling (dye electroporation and Kaede photoconversion) with supporting figures (1C-F). The data are internally consistent and methodologically sound.

result: V2b neurons in larval zebrafish (5-15 dpf) are exclusively inhibitory and comprise two stable subclasses based on neurotransmitter expression: V2b-gly neurons express only Glyt2 (~48% of population) and V2b-mixed neurons co-express Glyt2 and Gad1b (~52% of population). This pattern is stable from 5-15 dpf and differs from embryonic stages where V2b neurons are predominantly GABAergic.
evaluation: Claims C9-C13, C121, C58 describe neurotransmitter profiles with quantitative data (~91% Glyt2+, ~52% Gad1b+) across developmental stages (5, 10, 15 dpf). The manuscript provides direct evidence via transgenic marker coexpression (Figures 2A-C) and in situ validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The inference that all V2b neurons are inhibitory (C121) is well-supported since all express at least one inhibitory marker (Glyt2 and/or Gad1b).

result: GABAergic (V2b-mixed) and non-GABAergic (V2b-gly) V2b neurons show distinct spatial distributions: GABAergic somata are located slightly more ventrally on average but span the same dorsoventral range. Along the rostrocaudal axis, GABAergic V2b cells are most prevalent rostrally (~80%) and decrease to ~50% by midbody, while Glyt2 expression is consistent throughout the spinal cord.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 describe spatial distribution patterns with quantitative data and statistical analysis (Figure 2D-E, p=1.87×10⁻³). The manuscript provides direct measurements of soma position relative to spinal boundaries and rostrocaudal segments. The data are internally consistent and support the existence of distinct spatial patterns.

result: V2b-mixed and V2b-gly neurons exhibit distinct axonal trajectories in the dorsoventral axis: V2b-mixed axons project ventrally (DV 0.24-0.33) regardless of soma position, while V2b-gly axons project more dorsally (DV 0.31-0.65) with axon position correlated to soma position (r²=0.33, p<0.05). The two subclasses have similar numbers of collaterals but innervate largely distinct DV regions, overlapping with two peaks in motor neuron density.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20, C100-C101, C122 describe differential axon trajectories with quantitative anatomical data from single-cell fills (n=12 each subtype, Figure 3). The manuscript provides correlation analysis, statistical comparisons, and relates V2b axon position to motor neuron distribution. The data are methodologically sound with appropriate controls and replication.

result: V2b neurons form monosynaptic inhibitory connections onto motor neurons: optogenetic activation of V2b neurons elicits action potentials in V2b cells and robust IPSCs in motor neurons (median conductance 139 pS, 25-75% range 97-174 pS). Multiple control experiments confirm these IPSCs arise from V2b rather than CSF-cN neurons.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 establish V2b-to-motor neuron connectivity through optogenetic activation paired with electrophysiology. The manuscript provides validation of CatCh efficacy (Figure 4A), quantitative IPSC measurements (Figure 4D-E), and multiple controls including spatially targeted illumination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C) and recordings in animals with minimal V2b CatCh expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E). The convergent evidence strongly supports monosynaptic connectivity.

result: V2b-mediated inhibition onto motor neurons is differentially mediated by glycine and GABA depending on motor neuron type: strychnine blocks 91% of V2b-evoked IPSCs in fast motor neurons but only 71% in slow motor neurons (p=0.003), with gabazine eliminating the remainder in all cases. This indicates V2b-gly neurons preferentially inhibit fast motor neurons via glycinergic transmission, while V2b-mixed neurons inhibit slow motor neurons via mixed glycinergic/GABAergic transmission.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 describe pharmacological dissection of V2b-mediated inhibition with quantitative data and statistical analysis (Figure 4D-E, Wilcoxon Rank test p=0.003). The manuscript provides direct pharmacological evidence with appropriate receptor antagonists and relates findings to the anatomical data on V2b subclasses. The inference about differential targeting (C31-C32) is well-supported by converging anatomical and pharmacological evidence.

result: V2b activation does not robustly suppress motor neuron spiking: on average, V2b activation did not change spike thresholds or gain relationships in fast or slow motor neurons. Only 3/14 fast motor neurons showed increased spike threshold during V2b activation, and strychnine abolished this effect in 2/3 tested neurons.
evaluation: Claims C33, C108-C110 describe the limited effect of V2b activation on motor neuron spiking with quantitative data (Figure 4F). The manuscript provides direct electrophysiological measurements during concurrent V2b activation and motor neuron current injection. The authors appropriately acknowledge this unexpected finding and discuss potential explanations (dendritic vs. somatic effects).

result: V2b neurons form inhibitory connections within the V2b population: optogenetic activation of rostral V2b neurons evoked IPSCs in 52% (11/21) of midbody V2b neurons with median conductance 158 pS (25-75% range 84-203 pS). Strychnine blocked 80% of these IPSCs, with gabazine eliminating the remainder, indicating V2b-to-V2b connections form a disinhibitory pathway.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 establish V2b-to-V2b connectivity through optogenetic activation paired with V2b recordings (Figure 5A-C). The manuscript provides quantitative connectivity data (52% connection probability) and pharmacological characterization. The inference of a disinhibitory pathway (C37) is appropriately cautious and supported by the data.

result: V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons are indistinguishable by intrinsic electrophysiological properties: both subpopulations are silent at rest, show no differences in input resistance or spike shape, and typically fire only one or a few spikes during depolarizing current steps (only 3/10 V2b-gly and 3/9 V2b-mixed sustained spiking). Spikes are small in amplitude, similar to zebrafish V1 neurons.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C111-C112 describe intrinsic V2b physiology with quantitative comparisons between subclasses (Figure 5D-G). The manuscript provides direct electrophysiological measurements from identified V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons with appropriate statistical comparisons. The conclusion that subclasses are indistinguishable by intrinsic properties (C41) is well-supported despite their anatomical differences.

result: A CRISPR-generated Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP) knock-in line shows robust ZipACR expression in V2b neurons and ISN but only sparse, dim expression in CSF-cN apical extensions (not somata). Under low-intensity light conditions matching behavioral experiments, action potentials were completely or partially suppressed in 5/6 V2b cells but only 1/5 CSF-cNs.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 describe the ZipACR knock-in line and validate its cell-type specificity through imaging (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and electrophysiology (Figure 6B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The manuscript provides quantitative validation data showing differential suppression efficacy between V2b and CSF-cN neurons, which is critical for interpreting behavioral experiments.

result: Optogenetic suppression of V2b neurons increases locomotor frequency: tail beat frequency increased by 1.4 Hz (from 13.4 to 14.7 Hz, p=0.0025) in Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP)+ animals during light stimulation but not in ZipACR-negative siblings, while total tail displacement and movement quantity were unchanged. This effect was observed across three clutches.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49, C60 describe behavioral effects of V2b suppression with quantitative data and statistical analysis (Figure 6D-G, paired t-test p=0.0025). The manuscript provides appropriate controls (ZipACR-negative siblings) and replication across clutches. The specificity for V2b is supported by the ZipACR expression pattern and electrophysiological validation (C44-C45).

result: Optogenetic activation of V2b neurons reduces locomotor frequency: rostral V2b activation decreased the first inter-burst interval (p=1.72×10⁻⁴) and overall swim bout frequency (p=1.51×10⁻³) during fictive locomotion. Multiple controls (caudal stimulation, low V2b CatCh expression, red-shifted light) showed no effect on frequency, confirming specificity for V2b activation. V2b activation also reduced swim bout duration (p=4.65×10⁻³).
evaluation: Claims C50-C56, C61 describe behavioral effects of V2b activation with quantitative data and statistical analysis (Figure 7D-I). The manuscript provides multiple rigorous controls to exclude contributions from CSF-cN neurons and visual effects. The convergent evidence from suppression (C49) and activation (C56) experiments strongly supports a role for V2b neurons in speed control.

result: V2b neurons act as a brake on locomotor frequency and play a role in speed control: the bidirectional optogenetic manipulation experiments (suppression increases frequency, activation decreases frequency) provide evidence that V2b neurons serve as a brake on axial motor circuits, indicating a role for ipsilateral inhibition in speed control.
evaluation: Claims C57, C62-C63, C125 represent the main functional conclusion integrating results from both optogenetic manipulation experiments. The bidirectional effects (C49 and C56) provide strong converging evidence for this conclusion. The manuscript appropriately interprets these findings in the context of ipsilateral inhibition and speed control, though the exact mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

result: V2b subclasses synapse directly onto motor neurons with differential targeting to speed-specific circuits: V2b-gly neurons preferentially inhibit dorsally located fast motor neurons (predominantly glycinergic transmission), while V2b-mixed neurons inhibit ventrally located slow motor neurons (mixed glycinergic/GABAergic transmission).
evaluation: Claims C59, C106-C107 represent an inference integrating anatomical (C17-C20) and pharmacological (C28-C32) data. While the anatomical data show differential DV targeting and the pharmacological data show differential neurotransmitter sensitivity, the manuscript acknowledges a critical caveat (C81): fast and slow motor neurons have overlapping dendritic fields despite different somatic positions. This raises the possibility that differential receptor expression rather than anatomical targeting explains the pharmacological results. Direct paired recordings or higher-resolution anatomical experiments would be needed to definitively establish differential synaptic targeting.

result: V2b neurons are conserved across species: zebrafish and mouse V2b neurons are both inhibitory with ipsilateral, caudal axons. Gata3+ V2b neurons are present in vertebrates and marine annelids. Neurotransmitter profiles vary developmentally and across species, with embryonic zebrafish V2b neurons predominantly GABAergic, larval zebrafish predominantly glycinergic with ~50% GABAergic, and postnatal mouse V2b neurons nearly all glycinergic with ~25% GABAergic.
evaluation: Claims C64-C71 summarize comparative findings, primarily based on cited literature. The manuscript appropriately cites references for mouse V2b anatomy (C66), vertebrate and annelid presence (C67-C68), and developmental neurotransmitter profiles (C69-C71). The comparison to the current findings (C64-C65) is well-supported by the data presented.

result: V2b subclasses relate to previously identified spinal interneuron populations: the finding of V2b subclasses parallels subclasses in V0, V1, and V2a populations. V2b neurons may correlate to VeLD neurons, with V2b-mixed representing mature VeLDs and V2b-gly potentially representing a distinct or later-developing population. The relationship to V2c/V2s neurons remains unclear pending further investigation of Sox1a/b expression.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 discuss the relationship of V2b subclasses to other spinal interneuron populations, primarily based on cited literature and comparative analysis. The manuscript appropriately cites references for subclasses in other populations (C73), VeLD neurons (C74), V2c neurons (C75-C76), and V2s neurons (C77). The discussion is appropriately cautious about the relationship to V2c/V2s neurons, acknowledging the need for further investigation.

result: The manuscript discusses V2b function in the context of broader principles of spinal motor control: speed-dependent recruitment of interneurons, differential kinetics of glycine vs. GABA receptors, overlapping motor neuron dendritic fields, roles of ipsilateral inhibition in flexor-extensor alternation and speed control, effects of V1 ablation, in-phase inhibition during movement, and behavior-specific inhibition. These discussions contextualize the V2b findings within existing literature.
evaluation: Claims C78-C86, C123-C124, C126 represent discussion points contextualizing the findings, primarily based on cited literature. The manuscript appropriately cites references for each principle discussed. These claims are speculative or interpretive in nature (especially C124, C126) but are appropriately presented as such and grounded in the literature.

result: The manuscript describes additional cell types and experimental context relevant to interpreting V2b findings: Gata3 is also expressed in CSF-cN and ISN neurons with distinct anatomical features; CSF-cN have short ascending axons and limited motor neuron connectivity; motor neurons are organized by speed with dorsal neurons recruited for fast movements and ventral for slow; NMDA induces fictive locomotion; CSF-cN and serotonin have distinct effects on locomotor behavior.
evaluation: Claims C91-C94, C102-C105, C113-C118 provide essential context for interpreting the main findings, primarily based on cited literature and anatomical observations. The manuscript appropriately cites references for CSF-cN anatomy and function (C91-C94, C103, C114, C118), motor neuron organization (C104-C105), NMDA effects (C113), and serotonin effects (C115-C116). These contextual claims are well-supported and critical for experimental design and interpretation.
